summary: Steel lookout on Chase Mountain near Klamath Falls, built 1951 after a 1928 living-quarters cabin; no longer staffed and now carries equipment; NHLR US 485.

facts.design: All-steel tower with cab and catwalk, built 1951

access.note: Reached by gravel road from Highway 66; the tower now carries equipment and cameras, so it is a site to view rather than a lookout to climb

events.note: Lookout Reuben Gardner reported several forest fires
Lookout cabin planned for the summit; Willhite thinks an observation platform on a 12-by-12 frame cabin was built; construction date unclear
Ground cabin built for living quarters
Lookout staffed for 180 days, reporting by radio and telephone to Clover Station
Thelma Duke became the first woman lookout stationed in the area
Logging-train spark set fire to a Weyerhaeuser trestle near Spencer Creek; association lookouts sighted the smoke
New all-steel 20-foot tower; NHLR gives Holland Sheet Metal Co. as builder; Willhite gives Pade and Holland of Klamath Falls
Older 10-by-10 ground house moved to a nearby butte (Hambelton Butte); NHLR dates the move to 1949
Living quarters dismantled after falling into decay
Remodeled with new windows and flooring

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Firelookout and Cherylhill give the tower as 20 feet (6.1 m). The NHLR gives 21 feet. The record's 6.1 m was kept.
The NHLR gives 6,286 ft (1,916 m), which matches the record. Firelookout and Cherylhill give 6,349 ft. The record was left unchanged.
The NHLR dates the move of the old living building to Hambelton Butte to 1949. Willhite and Firelookout place it with the 1951 tower. The story gives the NHLR date and the 1951 date.
Willhite and the Forest Lookouts page list a new tower in 1935. The NHLR and Cherylhill date the standing steel tower to 1951 and do not mention a 1935 tower.
The NHLR describes a 12-by-12 cab. Willhite quotes a 1951 price for a 14-by-14 house on a 20-foot tower. The story does not give a cab size.

notes_for_editor: Staffing: Cherylhill's June 2022 visit and the July 2026 directory both say unmanned. One undated search snippet (peakbagging.com) says it is staffed in fire season; I did not read that page, so it is not used. Access is set to public because the directory counts the site as legally accessible; the story tells readers to view the tower from the road because it now holds equipment. The 1935 tower and the 1949 vs 1951 move are left as conflicts for the editor. No photos added.
